scenes.title: Navigating Multi-Hop Questions in RAG
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain why single-shot RAG fails on multi-hop questions and introduce architectural patterns to address this, emphasizing that it's a retrieval problem.
scenes.necessity: Many real-world questions require combining information from multiple sources through several 'hops' of reasoning or retrieval. Single-shot RAG often fails to provide complete answers for these complex queries.
scenes.story: Imagine you're trying to find a specific book in a massive library. You know the book's author, but you only know the author's *friend's* name. If you just walk up to the librarian and ask for 'the book by the friend of [friend's name]', they won't know what you mean. You first need to ask, 'Who is the friend of [friend's name]?' – that's your first hop. Once you have the author's name, then you can ask, 'What books did [author's name] write?' – that's your second hop. A single, direct question won't get you there. This is a perfect analogy for 'multi-hop' questions in RAG.
scenes.narration:
RAG में Multi-Hop Questions को कैसे हल करते हैं?

यहाँ पहले कॉलेज का नाम पता करना होगा, फिर उसका राज्य!
बिल्कुल! एक सर्च में दोनों नहीं मिलेंगे। इसलिए AI पहले सवाल को तोड़ता है (Sub-query decomposition)। पहले ढूंढता है 'आईआईटी खड़गपुर', और फिर दूसरी सर्च करता है 'खड़गपुर किस राज्य में है'।
और दोनों टुकड़ों को जोड़कर जवाब दे देता है?
हाँ! इसे Multi-Hop Retrieval कहते हैं।
scenes.question: How do you handle multi-hop questions in RAG, where the answer requires combining information from several documents?
scenes.interview_question: How do you handle multi-hop questions in RAG, where the answer requires combining information from several documents?
scenes.interview_view:
Single-shot retrieval often fails on multi-hop questions because the initial query only captures the first 'hop'. For example, 'What company did the founder of X later start?' requires first identifying the founder of X, then searching for their subsequent company. Common patterns to handle this include: query decomposition (breaking the question into sub-questions, retrieving for each, then synthesizing), iterative/agentic retrieval (retrieving, reasoning about missing information, then issuing follow-up retrievals, similar to ReAct applied to RAG), and GraphRAG-style traversal when hops follow explicit entity relationships. The key insight is recognizing that multi-hop failures are a retrieval-architecture problem, not a generation problem, as the necessary evidence wasn't surfaced in the first place.

Which metrics would you use to evaluate retrieval and final answer quality?
What production trade-off would make you choose a different approach?

scenes.title: Navigating Conflicting Information in RAG
scenes.teaching_intent: To teach strategies for handling conflicting information from retrieved sources, focusing on transparency, metadata utilization, and data hygiene.
scenes.necessity: It's common for retrieved documents to contain conflicting information, especially in large, diverse corpora. Silently picking one side can lead to misinformation; a robust RAG system needs to explicitly address these conflicts.
scenes.story: Imagine you're building a news aggregator, and you retrieve two articles about the same event. One article, from a highly reputable source, says 'X happened.' Another article, from a less reliable blog, says 'Y happened.' If your system just blends these into a single answer, or silently picks one, it could spread misinformation. You wouldn't just pick a side without acknowledging the disagreement, right? You'd want to highlight the conflict, maybe explain why one source is more credible, or at least present both perspectives. This is the challenge of conflicting information in RAG.
scenes.narration:
अगर दो फाइलों में उल्टी-सीधी बातें लिखी हों, तो RAG किसका यकीन करेगा?
ये बहुत आम समस्या है दोस्त! मान लो एक पुरानी 2021 की पॉलिसी कहती है 'रिफंड 7 दिन में मिलेगा' और 2024 की नई पॉलिसी कहती है 'रिफंड 14 दिन में मिलेगा'।
अब AI बेचारा क्या करे?
अगर तुमने Metadata में तारीख सेव की है, तो AI हमेशा लेटेस्ट तारीख वाले डॉक्यूमेंट को प्राथमिकता देगा। और प्रॉम्प्ट में लिखो — 'अगर मतभेद दिखे, तो दोनों का जिक्र करो और बताओ कि नया नियम क्या है!'
वाह! इससे कस्टमर को कोई कन्फ्यूजन नहीं होगा।
scenes.question: How do you handle conflicting information across retrieved sources in a RAG system?
scenes.interview_question: How do you handle conflicting information across retrieved sources in a RAG system?
scenes.interview_view:
When retrieved sources conflict in a RAG system, the first step is to surface the conflict rather than silently picking one side. Instruct the model to explicitly note disagreements and, where possible, attribute each claim to its specific source. Source metadata can help resolve conflicts programmatically: prefer newer documents for time-sensitive facts (recency), prioritize official policy documents over informal communications (source authority/trust tier), and use document versioning to filter out or down-weight superseded content at retrieval time. Critically, maintaining data hygiene in the underlying corpus—through deduplication and deprecation of stale documents at ingestion—prevents many conflicts from ever reaching the retrieval stage, which is more reliable than post-hoc resolution.

scenes.title: RAG vs. Long Context Windows: A Strategic Choice
scenes.teaching_intent: To clarify why RAG remains crucial even with very long context window models, highlighting its distinct advantages in cost, freshness, precision, and access control.
scenes.necessity: With LLMs now supporting extremely long context windows, one might wonder if RAG is still necessary. Understanding the specific advantages of RAG over simply stuffing all information into the context is crucial for making informed architectural decisions.
scenes.story: Imagine you have a super-intelligent assistant who can read and remember an entire library's worth of books. You *could* give them the entire library every time you ask a question. But think about it: every time you ask, they have to 're-read' or at least 're-scan' that entire library. That's going to take a lot of time and cost a lot of money, even if they're fast. And what if a new book is added, or an old one is updated? You'd have to give them the whole updated library again. Now, what if instead, you had a librarian who could quickly find *only* the few relevant pages from *any* book in the library, and then give *just those pages* to your assistant? That's the core difference between a very long context window and RAG.
scenes.narration:
RAG vs Long Context Windows — जब मॉडल 10 लाख शब्द एक साथ पढ़ सकता है, तो क्या RAG की छुट्टी हो गई?
बिल्कुल नहीं दोस्त! सोचो तुम्हारे पास 10,000 किताबें हैं। क्या तुम हर बार पूरा कमरा भरकर किताबें LLM को भेजोगी?
नहीं, इसमें तो लाखों रुपये का बिल आ जाएगा और जवाब आने में 2 मिनट लगेंगे!
एक्जेक्टली! RAG एक सस्ता और तेज फिल्टर है। वो 10,000 में से सिर्फ 5 जरूरी पन्ने छांटता है। और वो 5 पन्ने तुम लॉन्ग-कॉन्टेक्स्ट मॉडल को दे दो। दोनों एक दूसरे के दोस्त हैं, दुश्मन नहीं!
scenes.question: RAG vs. a very long context window model — when would you still choose RAG even if the model could fit everything in context?
scenes.interview_question: RAG vs. a very long context window model — when would you still choose RAG even if the model could fit everything in context?
scenes.interview_view:
Even with very long context window models, RAG is often preferred due to several key advantages. Firstly, **cost and latency**: stuffing a huge corpus into every prompt means paying for and waiting on those input tokens on every query, whereas RAG's targeted retrieval is far cheaper and faster at scale. Secondly, **freshness and maintainability**: updating a vector index when a document changes is simpler and cheaper than re-processing a giant static context, and avoids needing to re-run everything through the model. Thirdly, **precision and traceability**: retrieval provides an explicit, auditable set of source chunks for grounding claims; models with large context windows are less reliable at pinpointing and using information 'lost in the middle' compared to targeted retrieval. Lastly, **access control**: RAG allows per-query filtering by permissions, which is much harder to enforce cleanly when an entire corpus is pre-loaded into context. In practice, many production systems combine both, using RAG to narrow down to a relevant working set, with a longer context window providing headroom.

scenes.title: LoRA: The Smart Way to Fine-Tune LLMs
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain LoRA's mechanism and its significant practical benefits in making large language model fine-tuning more accessible and efficient.
scenes.necessity: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) traditionally requires immense computational resources, making it impractical for many use cases. A method to significantly reduce these requirements while maintaining performance is essential.
scenes.story: Imagine you have a massive, incredibly complex painting. You want to subtly change the mood or style of the painting for a specific art exhibition, but you don't want to repaint the entire thing from scratch, which would be incredibly difficult and expensive. What if you could just add a few small, transparent overlays or filters on top of key parts of the original painting? These overlays would slightly adjust the colors and tones, achieving the new look without touching the original masterpiece. This is the intuition behind LoRA. Instead of retraining every single parameter of a giant LLM, we 'add' small, learnable components.
scenes.narration:
LoRA क्या है दक्ष? ये AI इंजीनियर्स का इतना चहेता क्यों है?
LoRA यानी Low-Rank Adaptation! सोचो तुम्हारे पास 70 बिलियन पैरामीटर्स का एक विशाल मॉडल है। पूरे मॉडल को दोबारा ट्रेन करने में करोड़ों रुपये के GPU लगेंगे।
तो LoRA ने क्या कमाल किया?
LoRA कहता है — 'पुराने विशाल मॉडल को हाथ मत लगाओ, उसे फ्रीज कर दो! उसके बगल में दो बहुत पतली और छोटी मैट्रिक्स जोड़ दो — मैट्रिक्स A और मैट्रिक्स B!'
और सिर्फ उन छोटी पत्तियों को ट्रेन करो?
हाँ! कुल पैरामीटर्स का सिर्फ 0.1%! जो काम 8 महंगे GPU पर नहीं हो रहा था, वो अब एक छोटे GPU पर कुछ ही घंटों में हो जाता है। जादू जैसा!
scenes.question: What is LoRA, and why is it so widely used for fine-tuning LLMs?
scenes.interview_question: What is LoRA, and why is it so widely used for fine-tuning LLMs?
scenes.interview_view:
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method that freezes all original model weights and injects small trainable low-rank matrices (A and B, where the update is approximated as ΔW = BA, with rank `r` much smaller than the original dimensions) alongside key weight matrices, typically the attention projection layers. This approach works because weight updates during fine-tuning tend to have a low 'intrinsic rank', meaning the meaningful changes required to adapt a model to a new task don't necessitate updating every parameter with full freedom. By training only the small A/B matrices, LoRA cuts trainable parameters by orders of magnitude (often less than 1% of the full model). Practical benefits include: far less GPU memory needed (no optimizer states for frozen weights), much faster training, small checkpoint sizes (megabytes instead of gigabytes) making it easy to store/swap many task-specific adapters, and zero added latency at inference time because the adapter can be merged back into the base weights.

Interview perspective:
Explain the decision boundary between prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning. Cover dataset quality, training/inference cost, generalization, evaluation, rollback, and the risk of specializing the model when the real requirement is external knowledge or better orchestration.

How would you evaluate whether fine-tuning actually improved the system?
What failure or rollback strategy would you use?

scenes.title: QLoRA: Supercharging LoRA with Quantization
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain QLoRA as an advancement over LoRA, specifically how 4-bit quantization and other memory optimizations enable fine-tuning very large models on consumer-grade GPUs.
scenes.necessity: While LoRA significantly reduces fine-tuning resource requirements, even it can be too demanding for extremely large models (65B+ parameters) on single consumer GPUs. A further memory optimization is needed to push the boundaries of accessibility.
scenes.story: We just talked about LoRA, which is like adding a small, efficient attachment to a giant machine to customize it. But what if the giant machine itself is still too heavy or too big to even fit into your workshop, let alone attach something to it? What if you could make the *entire base machine* incredibly compact and lightweight, without losing its core functionality, and *then* add your small LoRA attachment? That's what QLoRA achieves. It's about taking that massive base model and making it super memory-efficient, so you can actually work with it on more modest hardware.

QLoRA क्या है? क्या ये LoRA का भी बाप है?
बिल्कुल दोस्त! LoRA ने पैरामीटर्स कम किए, लेकिन बेस मॉडल अभी भी 16-बिट में बहुत सारी GPU मेमोरी मांग रहा था।
तो QLoRA ने क्या किया?
QLoRA ने बेस मॉडल को 4-बिट NormalFloat में कंप्रेस कर दिया! और उसके ऊपर LoRA के एडॉप्टर लगा दिए। अब तुम एक 65 बिलियन का विशालकाय मॉडल एक सिंगल गेमिंग GPU पर फाइन-ट्यून कर सकती हो!
अरे वाह! यानी घर बैठे स्टूडेंट्स भी बड़े मॉडल्स ट्रेन कर सकते हैं।
scenes.question: What is QLoRA, and how does it differ from standard LoRA?
scenes.interview_question: What is QLoRA, and how does it differ from standard LoRA?
scenes.interview_view:
QLoRA combines LoRA with 4-bit quantization of the frozen base model weights. It utilizes a specialized 4-bit NormalFloat data type, specifically designed for normally-distributed weights, along with double quantization and paged optimizers to efficiently manage memory spikes during training. In QLoRA, the base model remains frozen and quantized to 4-bit, drastically cutting its memory footprint. However, the small LoRA adapter matrices are still trained in higher precision (typically BF16), and gradients flow through the quantized weights during backpropagation without ever fully dequantizing them into memory. This innovation made it practical to fine-tune large models (65B+ parameters) on a single consumer or prosumer GPU, establishing QLoRA as a default choice when GPU memory is the primary constraint for a fine-tuning job.

scenes.title: Fine-Tuning vs. Prompting/RAG: Choosing the Right Tool
scenes.teaching_intent: To help the learner understand the distinct use cases for fine-tuning versus prompting/RAG, emphasizing that fine-tuning is for patterns/behavior, not knowledge.
scenes.necessity: Developers often misuse fine-tuning for tasks better suited for prompting or RAG, leading to inefficient and suboptimal results. Clarifying when to use each approach is crucial for effective LLM application development.
scenes.story: Imagine you have a new employee. If you want them to follow a very specific script for customer calls, always use certain phrases, and fill out a form in a precise format, would you give them a huge manual to read every time (prompting)? Or would you put them through an intensive training program to bake those behaviors into their routine (fine-tuning)? Now, if they need to answer questions about constantly updated product details, would you make them memorize everything (fine-tuning)? Or give them access to an up-to-date database they can quickly search (RAG)? This analogy helps us understand when to fine-tune versus rely on prompting or RAG.
scenes.narration:
Fine-Tuning vs Prompting/RAG — अगर कंपनी का डेटा हर हफ्ते बदलता हो, तो क्या फाइन-ट्यूनिंग करें?
बिल्कुल कभी नहीं दोस्त! अगर तुम हर हफ्ते नया डेटा सिखाने के लिए मॉडल को फाइन-ट्यून करोगी, तो कंपनी दिवालिया हो जाएगी!
तो क्या करें?
RAG का इस्तेमाल करो! डेटाबेस में नई फाइल डालना सेकंड्स का काम है। फाइन-ट्यूनिंग तब की जाती है जब डेटा नहीं, बल्कि मॉडल का व्यवहार बदलना हो — जैसे उसे डॉक्टर की तरह प्रिस्क्रिप्शन लिखना सिखाना।
scenes.question: When should you fine-tune vs. rely on prompting/RAG? Give a concrete example.
scenes.interview_question: When should you fine-tune vs. rely on prompting/RAG? Give a concrete example.
scenes.interview_view:
Fine-tuning is appropriate when: you need a consistent output format or style at scale without repeating lengthy instructions (reducing prompt-token cost and latency), you're teaching a narrow skill the base model struggles with even with good prompting (e.g., specific structured extraction schema, domain-specific classification with many labels), or you need to reliably bake in a particular tone or persona. A crucial distinction is that you should *not* fine-tune to add knowledge; this is a common mistake. Fine-tuning teaches patterns and behavior, but is a poor and expensive way to inject new facts reliably, as models fine-tuned on new facts can still hallucinate or misremember. RAG retrieves facts at query time with a verifiable source and handles facts that change after training. Concrete example: A customer support bot that must always output a structured JSON ticket-classification with 40 specific internal categories is a good fine-tuning candidate (a narrow, repeated, format-heavy skill). A bot answering questions about your company's constantly-updated product documentation is a RAG candidate, not a fine-tuning one.

scenes.fact: Fine-tuning is appropriate when: you need a consistent output format or style at scale without repeating lengthy instructions (reducing prompt-token cost and latency), you're teaching a narrow skill the base model struggles with even with good prompting (e.g., specific structured extraction schema, domain-specific classification with many labels), or you need to reliably bake in a particular tone or persona. A crucial distinction is that you should *not* fine-tune to add knowledge; this is a common mistake. Fine-tuning teaches patterns and behavior, but is a poor and expensive way to inject new facts reliably, as models fine-tuned on new facts can still hallucinate or misremember. RAG retrieves facts at query time with a verifiable source and handles facts that change after training. Concrete example: A customer support bot that must always output a structured JSON ticket-classification with 40 specific internal categories is a good fine-tuning candidate (a narrow, repeated, format-heavy skill). A bot answering questions about your company's constantly-updated product documentation is a RAG candidate, not a fine-tuning one.
scenes.key_takeaway: Fine-tune for consistent patterns, styles, or narrow skills; use Prompting/RAG for adding knowledge or handling frequently changing facts.

scenes.title: Catastrophic Forgetting: The Downside of Over-Specialization
scenes.teaching_intent: To define catastrophic forgetting and provide practical mitigation strategies, emphasizing PEFT methods and balanced training.
scenes.necessity: Fine-tuning a model on a narrow task can inadvertently degrade its broader, general capabilities. Understanding and mitigating this 'catastrophic forgetting' is essential to preserve the value of a powerful base model.
scenes.story: Imagine a brilliant musician who can play many different instruments and genres. Now, they decide to focus *intensely* on mastering just one very specific style of music for a competition. They practice that one style non-stop, forgoing all others. After the competition, they might be incredibly good at that specific style, but they've lost their fluidity, their general skill, and even forgotten how to play some of the other instruments they once excelled at. That's catastrophic forgetting. When we fine-tune an LLM too narrowly, it can 'forget' its general intelligence.

हाँ दोस्त! इंसान भी तो ऐसा करते हैं ना? सोचो तुमने किसी बच्चे को दिन-रात सिर्फ कोडिंग सिखाई, और वो भूल गया कि सामान्य बातचीत कैसे करते हैं!
अरे! AI के साथ भी ऐसा होता है?
बिल्कुल! अगर तुम एक समझदार बेस मॉडल को सिर्फ मेडिकल डेटा पर बहुत ज्यादा ट्रेन कर दोगी, तो वो डॉक्टर तो बन जाएगा लेकिन उसकी सामान्य मैथ्स और रीज़निंग खत्म हो जाएगी।
तो इसे कैसे रोकते हैं?
ट्रेनिंग डेटा में थोड़ा सा पुराना जनरल डेटा भी मिलाकर रखते हैं, या LoRA का इस्तेमाल करते हैं ताकि ओरिजिनल दिमाग सुरक्षित रहे।
scenes.question: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you mitigate it during fine-tuning?
scenes.interview_question: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you mitigate it during fine-tuning?
scenes.interview_view:
Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning on a narrow new task degrades the model's previously strong general capabilities. For example, a model fine-tuned heavily on customer-support tickets might become worse at general reasoning or coding than the original base model. Mitigations include: using PEFT methods like LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, as freezing most weights naturally limits how much general behavior can shift; mixing a portion of general-purpose or instruction data into the fine-tuning set alongside the task-specific data to prevent over-specialization; using a lower learning rate and fewer epochs, as over-training on a small dataset is a common cause; and evaluating on held-out general benchmarks (not just the target task) before and after fine-tuning to catch regressions early.

Interview perspective:
Explain the decision boundary between prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning. Cover dataset quality, training/inference cost, generalization, evaluation, rollback, and the risk of specializing the model when the real requirement is external knowledge or better orchestration.

How would you evaluate whether fine-tuning actually improved the system?
What failure or rollback strategy would you use?

scenes.title: Preparing and Validating Fine-Tuning Datasets for Production
scenes.teaching_intent: To highlight the critical importance of high-quality, diverse, and well-validated datasets for successful fine-tuning in production, and common pitfalls to avoid.
scenes.necessity: The quality of a fine-tuning dataset directly impacts the model's performance in production. Improper preparation and validation can lead to overfitting, poor generalization, and unreliable real-world output. Therefore, robust data practices are essential.
scenes.story: Think about building a high-performance race car. You wouldn't just throw a bunch of random parts together, would you? Every component needs to be high-quality, precisely engineered, and tested to work together. Your fine-tuning dataset is like the blueprint and materials for your LLM. If your 'materials' are low quality, noisy, or incomplete, the 'car' you build won't perform well, no matter how good your 'engine' (the base LLM) is. This is why preparing and validating your fine-tuning dataset properly is absolutely critical for production use.

scenes.question: How do you prepare and validate a fine-tuning dataset for production use?
scenes.interview_question: How do you prepare and validate a fine-tuning dataset for production use?
scenes.interview_view:
To prepare and validate a fine-tuning dataset for production use, prioritize quality over quantity: a few thousand high-quality, diverse, correctly-labeled examples reliably outperform a much larger noisy dataset, as LLMs are highly sensitive to label noise. Ensure diversity across edge cases, input lengths, and phrasing to promote generalization rather than memorization of surface patterns; deduplicate near-identical examples to prevent training bias and overfitting. Crucially, hold out a representative validation and test split *before* training (beyond just monitoring train/loss curves). Additionally, build a small human-reviewed evaluation set that mirrors real production traffic patterns, because offline loss metrics often do not correlate well with real-world output quality.

scenes.title: Full Fine-tuning vs. PEFT: When to Go All In
scenes.teaching_intent: To help the learner understand the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and PEFT, and when the significant investment in full fine-tuning is justified.
scenes.necessity: In real-world AI projects, teams need to make informed decisions about fine-tuning strategies to balance performance, cost, and risk. Understanding when full fine-tuning is truly necessary, despite its drawbacks, is crucial.
scenes.story: Imagine you're leading an AI project, and you've got a powerful, pre-trained LLM. Now, your task is to make it an expert in a super niche domain – let's say, ancient Sanskrit legal texts, which have their own unique grammar and reasoning. You know you need to fine-tune it to adapt it. So, the big question arises: do you try to update *every single parameter* of this massive model, or do you opt for a more efficient, 'partial' update strategy like PEFT?
scenes.narration:

बहुत कम लोग करते हैं दोस्त! Full Fine-Tuning की जरूरत सिर्फ तब पड़ती है जब तुम बिल्कुल नई दुनिया में कदम रख रही हो — जैसे AI को पूरी तरह से बायो-इन्फॉर्मेटिक्स या किसी ऐसी भाषा में ढालना हो जो उसने कभी देखी ही न हो।
जहाँ उसका 90% दिमाग बदलना पड़े?
हाँ! लेकिन 99% प्रोडक्शन कामों के लिए PEFT यानी Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (जैसे LoRA) ही काफी होता है।
scenes.question: Full fine-tuning vs. PEFT (LoRA/QLoRA) — when does full fine-tuning actually win?
scenes.interview_question: Full fine-tuning vs. PEFT (LoRA/QLoRA) — when does full fine-tuning actually win?
scenes.interview_view:
Full fine-tuning updates every parameter, offering the model maximum flexibility to adapt. This approach is the right call when the target domain or task is very far from the base model's pretraining distribution — for example, a highly specialized scientific domain with its own vocabulary and reasoning patterns. Crucially, you also need a genuinely large, high-quality dataset to support it, as PEFT's restricted capacity can become a ceiling in such extreme cases. However, in practice, full fine-tuning is far more expensive, requiring much more GPU memory and leading to slower iteration. It also carries a higher risk of catastrophic forgetting. Because of this, most teams default to LoRA/QLoRA and only resort to full fine-tuning when they've empirically hit PEFT's performance ceiling on their specific task.

scenes.title: Generating Synthetic Data: Boosting Your Training Set
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain practical methods for generating synthetic data for fine-tuning and, more importantly, to highlight the critical need for quality control to avoid introducing systematic errors.
scenes.necessity: Labeled data is often a bottleneck in fine-tuning LLMs for specific tasks. Generating synthetic data offers a way to augment training sets, but it comes with inherent risks that must be managed.
scenes.story: Okay, so you've got this incredible LLM, and you want to fine-tune it for a really specific task, like generating highly creative ad copy for a niche product. You have a few great examples, but you know you need *way* more data to get the model performing at its best. Hiring people to write thousands of new ad copies is expensive and slow. So, what's your next move? How do you get more training data when you're short on labeled examples?
scenes.narration:
Synthetic Data क्या होता है? क्या AI अपने ही बनाए डेटा से सीख सकता है?
हाँ दोस्त! जब तुम्हारे पास असली इंसानों का लिखा डेटा कम पड़ जाए, तो तुम एक बहुत ताकतवर मॉडल (जैसे GPT-4) से कहती हो — 'मुझे इस टॉपिक पर 10,000 सवाल और जवाब बनाकर दो!'

scenes.question: How would you generate synthetic data for fine-tuning when you don't have enough labeled examples?
scenes.interview_question: How would you generate synthetic data for fine-tuning when you don't have enough labeled examples?
scenes.interview_view:
You can use a strong LLM to generate candidate (input, output) pairs. This can be done by paraphrasing existing real examples, generating variations to cover edge cases, or even having the model produce reasoning traces for distillation purposes. The hard part, however, is quality control. Synthetic data inherits and can even amplify the generator model's own biases and errors. Therefore, it needs rigorous filtering, which can include rule-based checks, using a second LLM as a judge, or human spot-review of a sample. Blindly training on unfiltered synthetic data is a common way to bake subtle systematic errors into a fine-tuned model. Best practice suggests mixing synthetic data with a smaller amount of real, human-verified examples, and always evaluating the fine-tuned model on a held-out set of *real* examples to catch any distributional gap.

scenes.title: Understanding Embeddings: The Language of Meaning for Machines
scenes.teaching_intent: To define embeddings intuitively and technically, and to explain the key factors that influence their quality for a specific task.
scenes.necessity: Embeddings are foundational to almost all GenAI systems, enabling semantic understanding and retrieval. A clear grasp of what they are and how to assess their quality is essential.
scenes.story: Okay, let's talk about something truly foundational to almost every GenAI system out there: embeddings. Think about it like this: how does a computer understand the *meaning* of words or sentences? It's not just about matching keywords. If I say 'cat' and 'feline', they're different words, but they mean very similar things. If I say 'cat' and 'car', they're different in meaning. How do you quantify that 'sameness' or 'difference' in a way a machine can process?

'सेब' और 'केला' दोनों फल हैं, तो वो स्पेस में पास-पास खड़े होंगे?

एक्जेक्टली! इसी से कंप्यूटर शब्दों के रिश्ते और भावनाएं पकड़ता है।
scenes.question: What is an embedding, and what determines embedding quality for a given task?
scenes.interview_question: What is an embedding, and what determines embedding quality for a given task?
scenes.interview_view:
An embedding is a dense numerical vector representation of text, or even image/audio, in a high-dimensional space. It's produced by a model specifically trained so that semantically similar inputs map to nearby vectors in this space. This 'nearness' is typically measured by metrics like cosine similarity or dot product. The quality of an embedding for a given task depends on several factors: first, what the embedding model was trained on – a strong domain match is crucial. A general web-trained model might struggle with legal or medical jargon, unlike a domain-tuned one. Second, the training objective matters, with contrastive learning on similar/dissimilar pairs being a standard approach. Third, dimensionality plays a role; higher isn't always better as it can increase storage/compute cost and add noise. Finally, it's vital to evaluate embeddings using a task-relevant benchmark like MTEB, rather than just relying on vendor marketing.

scenes.title: Scaling Vector Search: HNSW, IVF, and Brute-Force
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain the core mechanisms and trade-offs of different vector similarity search algorithms, emphasizing why approximate methods are essential for scale.
scenes.necessity: As datasets grow to millions or billions of vectors, brute-force search becomes impractical, demanding efficient approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms.
scenes.story: You have a database of a billion product images. A customer uploads an image and wants to find visually similar products. If you compare it to *every single one* of the billion images, it will take forever! How do you find similar images *fast*?

हाँ, बहुत समय लगेगा!

scenes.question: Compare HNSW, IVF, and exact (brute-force) search for vector similarity search.
scenes.interview_question: Compare HNSW, IVF, and exact (brute-force) search for vector similarity search.
scenes.interview_view:
Brute-force, or exact search, compares the query vector to every single vector in the dataset. It's perfectly accurate, giving 100% recall, but its time complexity is O(n) per query, making it far too slow for datasets with millions or billions of vectors. IVF, or Inverted File Index, works by clustering vectors into partitions using k-means during index creation. At query time, it only searches the nearest few clusters instead of the entire dataset. This makes it much faster, with a tunable accuracy/speed tradeoff, but it requires an initial training/clustering step and can sometimes miss results near cluster boundaries. HNSW, or Hierarchical Navigable Small World, builds a multi-layer graph structure where each vector is a node connected to its approximate nearest neighbors. Search greedily traverses from sparse upper layers down to dense lower layers. HNSW achieves excellent recall/speed tradeoffs and is the most widely used Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithm in modern vector databases. Its main costs are higher memory overhead for the graph structure and slower index build/insert times compared to IVF. All three methods involve tradeoffs between recall, latency, memory, and build time. Approximate methods like HNSW and IVF are what make sub-100ms search over billions of vectors feasible in production, at the cost of a small, tunable amount of retrieval accuracy versus exact search.

HNSW achieves excellent recall/speed tradeoffs and is the most widely used Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithm in modern vector databases. Its main costs are higher memory overhead for the graph structure and slower index build/insert times compared to IVF. All three methods involve tradeoffs between recall, latency, memory, and build time. Approximate methods like HNSW and IVF are what make sub-100ms search over billions of vectors feasible in production, at the cost of a small, tunable amount of retrieval accuracy versus exact search.
scenes.key_takeaway: HNSW and IVF are approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms that trade a small, tunable loss in accuracy for massive speed gains, making vector search feasible at production scale where brute-force fails.

scenes.title: Choosing Your Vector Infrastructure: Dedicated vs. Integrated
scenes.teaching_intent: To guide the learner through the practical decision-making process of selecting vector search infrastructure by highlighting the trade-offs between dedicated vector databases and extensions to existing databases.
scenes.necessity: Deploying vector search in production requires choosing the right infrastructure. This decision involves balancing performance, scalability, operational complexity, and integration with existing systems.
scenes.story: Okay, you've decided to implement vector search for your application. Now, your team is discussing where to store these vectors. One engineer suggests using `pgvector` because you already use PostgreSQL. Another argues for a dedicated system like Pinecone. Both options seem viable, but which one is truly right for *your* project?

scenes.question: How do you choose between a dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus) and a vector-capable extension on an existing database (pgvector, Elasticsearch, MongoDB Atlas)?
scenes.interview_question: How do you choose between a dedicated vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus) and a vector-capable extension on an existing database (pgvector, Elasticsearch, MongoDB Atlas)?
scenes.interview_view:
Dedicated vector databases are purpose-built for high-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search. They typically offer more mature filtering, hybrid search capabilities, and multi-tenancy features right out of the box. They are generally the better default when vector search is the core workload of your application, and you anticipate large scale – think tens of millions or more vectors, with high queries per second. On the other hand, vector-capable extensions like pgvector become compelling when you already use that specific database for your transactional data and want to avoid the operational overhead of running a second system. They are also a good fit when your scale is moderate, or when you need vector search tightly joined with existing relational data and require transactional guarantees (ACID) within the same query. The practical decision drivers include your existing infrastructure and team familiarity, your expected scale and latency SLAs, whether you need hybrid (metadata-filtered) search, and your tolerance for operational overhead. This is squarely a 'depends on constraints' answer, and interviewers want to see you reason through these tradeoffs.

scenes.title: Similarity Metrics: Cosine, Dot Product, and Euclidean Distance
scenes.teaching_intent: To differentiate between common vector similarity metrics (cosine, dot product, Euclidean) and emphasize the critical importance of matching the metric to how the embedding model was trained.
scenes.necessity: Choosing the correct similarity metric directly impacts the accuracy of retrieval systems. Understanding the nuances of each metric prevents silent degradation of search quality.
scenes.story: Alright, so we know embeddings represent meaning as vectors. But how do you actually *measure* the 'similarity' between two of these vectors? Is there just one way, or are there different ways to define 'similar'? Imagine two vectors pointing in roughly the same direction, but one is much longer than the other. Are they similar? Or what if they're the same length but pointing in slightly different directions? How do you quantify 'sameness' when magnitude and direction both play a role?
scenes.narration:
Similarity Metrics — Cosine, Dot Product और Euclidean Distance में क्या फर्क है?
बहुत सीधा फर्क है दोस्त! Cosine Similarity सिर्फ दिशा यानी Angle देखती है, लंबाई नहीं। जैसे दो लोग एक ही रास्ते पर चल रहे हैं, चाहे एक तेज चले और एक धीमे।
और Euclidean Distance?
वो दो बिंदुओं के बीच की सीधी दूरी (Straight line distance) नापती है। छोटी दूरी मतलब ज्यादा सिमिलैरिटी!
और Dot Product?
Dot Product दिशा और लंबाई दोनों को देखता है। अगर तुम्हारे वेक्टर्स Normalized यानी 1 लंबाई के हैं, तो Dot Product और Cosine बिल्कुल एक जैसे होते हैं!
scenes.question: What is the difference between cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean (L2) distance for vector search — and when does it matter which you pick?
scenes.interview_question: What is the difference between cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean (L2) distance for vector search — and when does it matter which you pick?
scenes.interview_view:
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, effectively ignoring their magnitude or length. It's excellent when only the direction or semantic orientation matters, not how 'strong' the vector is. Dot product, on the other hand, incorporates both the angle and the magnitude of the vectors. It's often the fastest to compute and is the correct choice when the embedding model was specifically trained to optimize dot product similarity, which many modern embedding models are. Euclidean, or L2 distance, measures the straight-line distance between the endpoints of two vectors in the high-dimensional space. It is very sensitive to magnitude and is more commonly used outside of text embeddings, for example, in clustering tasks. In practice, the golden rule is to match whichever metric the embedding model was trained and optimized with. Using cosine similarity on a model trained for dot product, or vice versa, can silently degrade retrieval quality, and this detail often distinguishes candidates who have actually shipped retrieval systems from those who haven't.

What production trade-off would make you choose a different approach?

scenes.title: Embedding Model Versioning: The Hidden Cost of Upgrades
scenes.teaching_intent: To highlight the significant operational challenges and costs associated with upgrading embedding models in production, emphasizing the need for a strategic approach like blue-green deployment.
scenes.necessity: In production systems, embedding models are constantly evolving. A robust strategy for versioning and upgrading these models is essential to maintain data consistency, search quality, and system availability.
scenes.story: Your team just released a brand new, super-improved embedding model! Everyone's excited. You want to swap out the old model in your production system immediately to get better search results. Can you just replace the old model file and expect everything to work seamlessly? What's the hidden cost, the real challenge here?
scenes.narration:
Embedding Model को अपग्रेड करने का 'Hidden Cost' क्या है?
दोस्त, कभी ऐसा मत करना कि आधा डेटा पुराने मॉडल से एम्बेड किया और नया डेटा नए मॉडल से! दोनों की दुनिया और नंबर्स बिल्कुल अलग होते हैं।
तो क्या पूरा डेटाबेस दोबारा बदलना पड़ेगा?
हाँ! अगर तुमने मॉडल बदला, तो पुराने सारे करोड़ों वेक्टर्स को डिलीट करके दोबारा री-एम्बेड करना पड़ेगा। इसमें लाखों रुपये की कम्प्यूटिंग और समय लगता है। इसलिए मॉडल सोच-समझकर चुनो!
scenes.question: How do you handle embedding model versioning — what happens when you upgrade to a newer/better embedding model?
scenes.interview_question: How do you handle embedding model versioning — what happens when you upgrade to a newer/better embedding model?
scenes.interview_view:
Here's the critical point: different embedding models produce vectors in *incompatible spaces*. This means you absolutely cannot mix vectors generated by two different models, or even different versions of the same model, in a single similarity search. A query embedded with model B will not meaningfully compare against documents embedded with model A. Therefore, upgrading an embedding model requires a full re-embedding of your entire corpus with the new model. This process is typically managed using a blue-green deployment pattern: you build a completely new index with the new model in parallel, validate its retrieval quality against your evaluation set, and then, only once confident, you cut traffic over to the new index. Trying to mutate the live index in place risks a period of inconsistent or degraded search quality. This is why embedding model choice is a much bigger commitment than it might first appear in a design discussion; re-embedding a large corpus has real cost and significant downtime or consistency implications, and experienced interviewers want to hear that you understand it's not a simple drop-in swap.

Discuss retrieval quality separately from answer quality, then mention evaluation, latency, freshness, and cost trade-offs.

Which metrics would you use to evaluate retrieval and final answer quality?
What production trade-off would make you choose a different approach?

scenes.title: Matryoshka Embeddings: Scalable Quality with Tunable Dimensions
scenes.teaching_intent: To introduce Matryoshka embeddings as a solution for achieving flexible storage/speed vs. accuracy tradeoffs from a single embedding model, enhancing production efficiency.
scenes.necessity: Managing the trade-off between embedding dimensionality (and thus quality) and the associated storage/compute costs is a key challenge in large-scale production systems. Matryoshka embeddings offer a flexible solution.
scenes.story: Okay, so you're successfully using embeddings, perhaps even high-dimensional ones like 1536 dimensions, and they're giving you fantastic retrieval quality. But, there's always a 'but', right? These high-dimensional vectors are quite large. They take up a lot of storage space, and running searches on them can be a bit slower. What if you need a faster, cheaper search for a massive corpus, but you don't want to train a whole new, smaller model? Is there a way to get 'smaller' embeddings from your 'big' ones without losing too much quality?
scenes.narration:
Matryoshka Embeddings क्या होती हैं? क्या ये रूसी गुड़िया जैसी हैं?

तो हम सिर्फ पहले 256 नंबर्स सेव कर सकते हैं?
हाँ! इससे तुम्हारा डेटाबेस 6 गुना छोटा हो जाएगा और स्पीड 10 गुना बढ़ जाएगी! और जब कभी बहुत बारीकी से फैसला करना हो, तब पूरे नंबर्स इस्तेमाल कर लो।
scenes.question: What are Matryoshka embeddings, and why are they useful in production?
scenes.interview_question: What are Matryoshka embeddings, and why are they useful in production?
scenes.interview_view:
Matryoshka Representation Learning is a technique that trains embeddings in such a way that meaningful semantic information is concentrated in the leading dimensions of the vector. This is the key insight: it means you can effectively 'truncate' a high-dimensional embedding – for example, reducing it from 1536 dimensions down to 256 dimensions – and still retain most of its retrieval quality. The magic here is that you don't need a separately-trained smaller model to do this. This capability gives a single embedding model a tunable storage/speed versus accuracy tradeoff at query time. You can use the full-dimension vector when maximum quality matters most, or switch to a truncated version for faster search and lower storage costs on huge corpora. This approach eliminates the need to maintain multiple models for different performance profiles. It's increasingly offered as a built-in option by modern embedding APIs and is a good signal of staying current if you can speak to it.

scenes.title: Defining AI Agents: Beyond Simple LLM Calls
scenes.teaching_intent: To clearly differentiate an AI agent from a basic LLM call or a fixed pipeline by emphasizing its dynamic decision-making and iterative observe-reason-act loop.
scenes.necessity: As GenAI applications evolve from simple Q&A to complex, multi-step workflows, understanding the concept of an 'agent' is fundamental for designing and building autonomous systems.
scenes.story: Alright, let's shift gears a bit and talk about AI Agents, which are becoming super central to GenAI engineering. Think about it: if I ask an LLM, 'What's the capital of France?', it gives me a direct answer. That's a simple LLM call. Now, what if I ask it to 'Find me the cheapest flight from Mumbai to London next Tuesday, book it, and then send me the confirmation email'? That's a completely different level of complexity, right? A simple LLM call can't just 'do' that.
scenes.narration:
एक AI Agent सिर्फ एक नॉर्मल LLM कॉल से कैसे अलग होता है?
नॉर्मल LLM एक सवाल का एक जवाब देकर सो जाता है दोस्त। लेकिन एक AI Agent के पास 4 चीजें होती हैं: Perception (देखना), Brain (प्लान बनाना), Tools (काम करना), और Memory (याद रखना)!
मतलब वो खुद से फैसले लेता है?
हाँ! तुम उससे कहो 'मेरी फ्लाइट बुक करो और होटल ढूंढो'। वो खुद सोचेगा, गूगल करेगा, सीट चेक करेगा, अगर टिकट न मिले तो दूसरा ऑप्शन ढूंढेगा, और काम खत्म करके तुम्हें बताएगा!
scenes.question: What defines an 'agent' as opposed to a simple LLM call or a fixed pipeline?
scenes.interview_question: What defines an 'agent' as opposed to a simple LLM call or a fixed pipeline?
scenes.interview_view:
An agent uses an LLM to dynamically decide its own sequence of actions. This means it figures out which tools to call, in what order, and when to stop, all based on intermediate results. It doesn't follow a hardcoded, predetermined sequence of steps like a fixed pipeline. The defining loop of an agent is typically: observe the current state or context, then reason about what it should do next, then act by calling a tool, retrieving information, or formulating a response, then observe the result of that action, and repeat this loop until a stopping condition is met. This iterative, dynamic control flow is what enables agents to handle open-ended tasks that a fixed pipeline simply can't anticipate in advance. For example, a standard RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline is a fixed workflow (retrieve, then generate). But an agentic RAG system decides for itself whether to retrieve, what to search for, whether the results are sufficient, and whether to search again — the control flow itself is delegated to the model.

Interview perspective:
For a production answer, describe the control loop and boundaries: model decision, tool schema, authorization, execution, result validation, iteration limits, timeout/error handling, and observability. Also explain when a deterministic workflow is preferable to an agent.
interview_followups: When would you use a deterministic workflow instead of an agent?
How would you limit tool permissions and prevent unsafe actions?
How would you handle tool failure, loops, timeouts, and unexpected tool output?

scenes.title: Function/Tool Calling: The Safe Bridge to External Actions
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain the technical mechanism of LLM function/tool calling, emphasizing the structured communication and the critical safety separation between the model's intent and the application's execution.
scenes.necessity: Function/tool calling is fundamental for AI agents to interact with the real world. Understanding its mechanics and safety features is crucial for building robust and secure agentic systems.
scenes.story: Okay, so we just talked about agents dynamically deciding what to do. Often, 'what to do' means using a 'tool' – like searching the web, sending an email, or querying a database. But wait, an LLM is just a language model, a fancy text predictor. It can't actually *send an email* itself, right? So how does it 'use' these tools? How does the model communicate its intention to your application in a way that's both structured and safe?
scenes.narration:
Function Calling और Tool Calling क्या है? क्या LLM सीधे हमारा डेटाबेस डिलीट कर सकता है?
नहीं दोस्त, यही तो सबसे बड़ी खूबसूरती है! LLM सीधे कोई कोड रन नहीं करता। वो सिर्फ एक JSON पर्ची बनाकर देता है — 'कृपया getWeather(city="Delhi") फंक्शन चलाओ'!
और कोड कौन चलाता है?
कोड तुम्हारा अपना सुरक्षित बैकएंड सर्वर चलाता है! सर्वर वेदर चेक करता है और नतीजा LLM को वापस देता है। यानी चाबी हमेशा तुम्हारे हाथ में रहती है।
scenes.question: How does function/tool calling actually work under the hood?
scenes.interview_question: How does function/tool calling actually work under the hood?
scenes.interview_view:
Function or tool calling works by the application providing the LLM with a set of tool definitions. These definitions include the tool's name, a description of what it does, and a JSON schema of the expected parameters it takes. These definitions are sent alongside the user's prompt. The LLM, which has been trained or fine-tuned to recognize when a user's request maps to one of these tools, then outputs a structured call. This structured call includes the tool's name and the arguments that match its schema, often instead of, or alongside, natural language. Critically, the model *does not execute the tool itself*. It only generates the structured intent to call it. The application code then parses this structured output, actually executes the function or API call, and feeds the result back into the conversation as a new message. This allows the model to incorporate the result into its next response or decide on a subsequent action. This separation is a key safety property: the model proposes, but the application, with its permission and validation layers, disposes. This gives engineers a crucial checkpoint to validate arguments, enforce authorization, or even require human approval before any action is actually executed.

Interview perspective:
For a production answer, describe the control loop and boundaries: model decision, tool schema, authorization, execution, result validation, iteration limits, timeout/error handling, and observability. Also explain when a deterministic workflow is preferable to an agent.

How would you handle tool failure, loops, timeouts, and unexpected tool output?

This gives engineers a crucial checkpoint to validate arguments, enforce authorization, or even require human approval before any action is actually executed.
scenes.key_takeaway: Function/tool calling involves the application providing tool definitions to the LLM, which then outputs a structured call (intent). The application executes the tool, ensuring safety and control by separating the model's proposal from actual execution.

scenes.title: Taming Multi-Agent Chaos
scenes.teaching_intent: To make the learner understand the inherent challenges in multi-agent systems and the necessity of structural solutions to ensure stability and reliability.
scenes.necessity: Without clear rules and structure, multiple autonomous agents can quickly lead to unpredictable, chaotic, or erroneous behavior, making the system unusable in production.
scenes.story: Imagine you're trying to organize a group project with a bunch of very smart, but also very opinionated, friends. Everyone has great ideas, but no one has a clear role, no one knows who makes the final decision, and sometimes, people just keep trying the same thing over and over, even if it's not working. Sounds like a recipe for disaster, right? Yahin par the real problem starts.
scenes.narration:
Multi-Agent Systems में जब कई सारे एजेंट्स आपस में बात करते हैं, तो अफरा-तफरी कैसे रोकें?
सोचो एक कमरे में 5 लोग एक साथ चिल्ला रहे हों — कोई काम नहीं होगा! इसीलिए Multi-Agent में एक 'Supervisor' या 'Orchestrator' एजेंट बनाया जाता है।
जैसे टीम का मैनेजर?
बिल्कुल! मैनेजर रिसर्च वाले एजेंट को काम देता है, फिर उसका काम कोडर एजेंट को देता है, और रिव्यूअर एजेंट से चेक करवाता है। सबको अपनी सीमाएं पता होती हैं।
scenes.question: How do you handle a multi-agent system where agents might disagree, loop, or produce inconsistent results?
scenes.interview_question: How do you handle a multi-agent system where agents might disagree, loop, or produce inconsistent results?
scenes.interview_view:
To handle multi-agent systems effectively, define clear role boundaries and hand-off protocols up front, often with an orchestrator or supervisor agent routing tasks to specialist sub-agents and owning the final decision. Bound the system with hard stopping conditions like maximum iteration counts, timeouts, and explicit success/failure criteria to prevent reasoning loops. Use structured, typed hand-offs between agents to reduce miscommunication, and log/trace every step for debuggability, as multi-agent systems are notoriously hard to debug without strong observability.

Interview perspective:
For a production answer, describe the control loop and boundaries: model decision, tool schema, authorization, execution, result validation, iteration limits, timeout/error handling, and observability. Also explain when a deterministic workflow is preferable to an agent.

How would you limit tool permissions and prevent unsafe actions?
How would you handle tool failure, loops, timeouts, and unexpected tool output?

scenes.title: Measuring Agent Success in the Real World
scenes.teaching_intent: To highlight that evaluating an agent's performance in production goes beyond simple responses and requires a multi-faceted approach considering outcomes, process efficiency, and safety.
scenes.necessity: An agent might 'respond' but still fail to achieve its objective, operate inefficiently, or even pose safety risks in a live environment. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation framework is crucial.
scenes.story: Okay, so you've built an amazing LLM agent, and it's responding to user queries, doing its thing. But here's the real test: is it actually *working correctly* in the wild? I mean, it might give a plausible-sounding answer, but is that answer truly helpful? Is it taking five extra steps to get there? Or worse, is it accidentally trying to do something it shouldn't?
scenes.narration:
असली दुनिया में एजेंट सफल हुआ या फेल, ये कैसे नापते हैं?
दोस्त, लोग अक्सर सिर्फ 'सटीकता' देखते हैं। लेकिन असली दुनिया में 3 चीजें देखी जाती हैं: पहला — Task Completion Rate (क्या यूजर का असली काम पूरा हुआ?)
दूसरा क्या है?
Cost and Latency per task — ऐसा तो नहीं कि 10 रुपये का काम करने में 500 रुपये की API कॉल फूंक दीं और 5 मिनट लगा दिए!
और तीसरा?
Safety and Tool Error Rate — क्या उसने गलत टूल चलाकर डेटा तो नहीं बिगाड़ दिया? इन तीनों का संतुलन ही सफलता तय करता है।
scenes.question: How would you evaluate whether an agent is working correctly in production?
scenes.interview_question: How would you evaluate whether an agent is working correctly in production?
scenes.interview_view:
Evaluating an agent in production involves several metrics: task-level success rate against a labeled evaluation set (did it achieve the intended outcome, not just respond), trajectory/process metrics (number of steps, tool-call accuracy, recovery from errors), and safety/guardrail metrics (rate of unauthorized actions, correct human confirmation requests). This combines automated evaluation (LLM-as-judge) with human review of traces and production monitoring for anomalies.

How would you limit tool permissions and prevent unsafe actions?
How would you handle tool failure, loops, timeouts, and unexpected tool output?

scenes.title: Agent Safety: Designing Permissions and Guardrails
scenes.teaching_intent: To emphasize the critical need for robust security measures and guardrails to prevent LLM agents from executing destructive or unauthorized actions.
scenes.necessity: Giving an LLM agent access to tools, especially those with real-world impact, without strict controls is a major security risk. Agents can misinterpret or 'hallucinate' dangerous actions.
scenes.story: Imagine giving a new, very enthusiastic, but slightly naive intern full access to all your company's critical systems – the database, the email server, the payment system – without any supervision or limitations. What could possibly go wrong? Deleting critical data, sending unauthorized emails, making purchases without approval. Sounds like a nightmare, right? The same principle applies to LLM agents.
scenes.narration:
Agent Safety — एजेंट्स को टूल्स की परमिशन कैसे देनी चाहिए?
Principle of Least Privilege याद रखो दोस्त! किसी इंटर्न को पहले दिन बैंक का मास्टर पासवर्ड नहीं दिया जाता ना?
बिल्कुल नहीं! सिर्फ वही एक्सेस दो जो उसके काम के लिए जरूरी हो।
एजेंट के साथ भी यही करो! Read-only टूल्स (जैसे डेटा देखना) उसे खुद करने दो। लेकिन Destructive टूल्स (जैसे पैसे ट्रांसफर करना या डेटा डिलीट करना) के लिए हमेशा 'Human-in-the-loop' रखो — यानी स्क्रीन पर इंसान से 'Yes/No' कन्फर्मेशन मांगो!
scenes.question: How do you design tool permissions and guardrails so an agent can't take destructive or unauthorized actions?
scenes.interview_question: How do you design tool permissions and guardrails so an agent can't take destructive or unauthorized actions?
scenes.interview_view:
To prevent destructive actions, apply least-privilege at the tool level, scoping credentials to only what's necessary. Gate irreversible or high-stakes actions behind explicit human confirmation. Validate tool arguments server-side before execution, not blindly trusting the model's output. Finally, set hard boundaries the agent cannot reason its way around, such as rate limits, spend caps, and explicit denylists of forbidden actions.

Interview perspective:
For a production answer, describe the control loop and boundaries: model decision, tool schema, authorization, execution, result validation, iteration limits, timeout/error handling, and observability. Also explain when a deterministic workflow is preferable to an agent.
interview_followups: When would you use a deterministic workflow instead of an agent?
How would you limit tool permissions and prevent unsafe actions?
How would you handle tool failure, loops, timeouts, and unexpected tool output?

scenes.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Memory for Agents
scenes.teaching_intent: To clarify the distinction between short-term and long-term memory in agent systems, explaining their implementation and necessity due to LLM context window limitations.
scenes.necessity: LLMs have limited context windows, meaning they can't remember everything indefinitely. Agents need a way to retain crucial information across turns and sessions to maintain coherence and personalized experiences.
scenes.story: Think about talking to a person. You remember what they just said a few moments ago, right? That's your short-term memory. But you also remember their name, their preferences, and things they told you last week or even last year – that's your long-term memory. Now, imagine if every time you spoke to someone, they completely forgot everything you'd ever told them before that exact conversation. Frustrating, right? That's what an LLM without proper memory management would be like.
scenes.narration:
एजेंट्स की Short-Term और Long-Term Memory में क्या अंतर होता है?
Short-Term Memory है अभी चल रही बातचीत का कॉन्टेक्स्ट विंडो — जैसे अभी 2 मिनट पहले तुमने क्या कहा था।
और Long-Term Memory?
Long-Term Memory है डेटाबेस! जहाँ वो तुम्हारी पसंद, तुम्हारा नाम, और पिछले महीने की गई बातें याद रखता है। जब भी जरूरत होती है, वो वेक्टर सर्च करके पुरानी यादें निकाल लाता है।
scenes.question: What's the difference between short-term and long-term memory in an agent system, and how do you implement each?
scenes.interview_question: What's the difference between short-term and long-term memory in an agent system, and how do you implement each?
scenes.interview_view:
Short-term (working) memory is the current conversation/task context, typically held in the context window and discarded or summarized after the session. Long-term memory persists information across sessions (user preferences, past decisions), stored in a database or vector store, and selectively retrieved into the prompt when relevant. A common pattern is periodic summarization of old turns and writing durable facts to long-term storage.

scenes.title: Reducing LLM Inference Cost and Latency
scenes.teaching_intent: To equip the learner with practical strategies for optimizing LLM inference in production, focusing on cost and latency reduction.
scenes.necessity: Deploying LLMs at scale can be prohibitively expensive and slow. Optimizing these factors is crucial for making LLM applications economically viable and user-friendly.
scenes.story: You've built this amazing LLM-powered application, everyone loves it, and it's getting a ton of traffic. Awesome! But then you get your first cloud bill, and your jaw drops. And users start complaining about how slow it is sometimes. Suddenly, your cool app has a big problem: it's too expensive and too slow to run at scale.
scenes.narration:
LLM का बिल और लेटेंसी कम करने के सबसे असरदार तरीके क्या हैं?
दोस्त, 4 महामंत्र याद रखो: पहला — Semantic Caching! अगर 100 लोग एक ही सवाल पूछ रहे हैं, तो 100 बार LLM को कॉल मत करो, कैश से जवाब दे दो!
दूसरा मंत्र?
Model Tiering या Routing! आसान सवालों के लिए छोटा और सस्ता मॉडल (जैसे GPT-4o-mini) चलाओ, और जब कोई बहुत कठिन लॉजिक आए तभी बड़ा मॉडल बुलाओ।
तीसरा और चौथा?
तीसरा — प्रॉम्प्ट को छोटा रखो, फालतू शब्द काटो। और चौथा — स्ट्रक्चर्ड आउटपुट में सिर्फ जरूरी फील्ड्स ही मांगो!
scenes.question: What levers do you have to reduce LLM inference cost and latency in production?
scenes.interview_question: What levers do you have to reduce LLM inference cost and latency in production?
scenes.interview_view:
To reduce LLM inference cost and latency, levers include model selection (smallest model for quality bar, model routing), caching (exact, semantic, prompt KV cache reuse), serving optimizations (batching, quantization, speculative decoding, optimized inference servers like vLLM/TGI with PagedAttention), and prompt/context efficiency (trimming context, concise prompts, capping max output tokens).

Interview perspective:
Frame the answer as an engineering trade-off. Identify the latency/cost bottleneck, distinguish time-to-first-token from total latency and throughput, and discuss caching, batching, concurrency, timeouts, retries, rate limits, and graceful degradation where relevant.
interview_followups: What is the main bottleneck and how would you measure it?
How would your design behave under traffic spikes or provider throttling?
What would you optimize first if cost doubled without a quality change?
scenes.production_angle: Measure latency, throughput, error rate, token usage, and provider limits before optimizing.

scenes.title: Monitoring LLM Applications in Production
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain the unique challenges of monitoring LLM applications and what specific metrics and alerts are necessary to ensure quality, cost-efficiency, and user satisfaction.
scenes.necessity: Traditional monitoring focuses on uptime, but LLM systems can be 'up' while silently degrading in quality, increasing costs, or producing unsafe outputs. Specific LLM-centric monitoring is essential.
scenes.story: Your LLM application is running, and the server says 'OK'. Great, right? But then users start complaining, your cloud bill suddenly spikes, or the answers the AI gives become subtly worse over time. The system is 'up', but it's silently failing in ways that matter to your users and your business. How would you even know this is happening?
scenes.narration:
Production में LLM ऐप्स को मॉनिटर कैसे करते हैं? क्या नॉर्मल सर्वर मॉनिटरिंग काफी नहीं है?
नॉर्मल सर्वर सिर्फ कहेगा 'HTTP 200 OK' — यानी सर्वर चल रहा है। लेकिन अंदर AI कचरा जवाब दे रहा हो सकता है!
अरे! मतलब वो चेक नहीं कर पाता कि जवाब सही है या गलत?
बिल्कुल! इसलिए LLM मॉनिटरिंग में हम ट्रैक करते हैं: Token usage, Latency per token, User feedback (Thumbs up/down), और हैलुसिनेशन का रेट।
ताकि क्वालिटी गिरते ही तुरंत अलर्ट आ जाए?
हाँ, Langfuse या Arize जैसे टूल्स से रियल-टाइम डैशबोर्ड पर सब दिखता रहता है।
scenes.question: How do you monitor an LLM application in production? What should trigger an alert?
scenes.interview_question: How do you monitor an LLM application in production? What should trigger an alert?
scenes.interview_view:
Monitor latency (p50/p95/p99, time-to-first-token), error/failure rates, cost per request and daily spend, and token usage patterns. Track quality signals like automated groundedness/faithfulness scoring, user feedback (thumbs up/down), and drift detection. Alerting should be tied to user/business impact: latency SLA breaches, error rate spikes, cost anomalies (e.g., prompt-injection loops), and sudden drops in user satisfaction.

scenes.title: LLM Observability and Tracing: A Different Beast
scenes.teaching_intent: To distinguish LLM observability from traditional software observability, highlighting the need to trace the full reasoning path in non-deterministic, multi-step LLM systems for effective debugging.
scenes.necessity: Traditional software tracing is designed for deterministic code paths. LLMs are non-deterministic and involve complex multi-step chains, making traditional methods inadequate for debugging their failures.
scenes.story: When a regular software application crashes, you can often look at a stack trace and pinpoint exactly where the code broke. It's usually a predictable path. But what if an LLM gives a wrong answer? It's not a 'crash'. It's a 'misunderstanding'. Was it the retrieval step that pulled bad information? Was the prompt poorly phrased? Did the model 'reason' incorrectly? It's like a detective story where you need to see every thought process, not just the final action.
scenes.narration:
LLM Observability और Tracing क्या है? ये एक अलग जानवर क्यों है?
दोस्त, नॉर्मल सॉफ्टवेयर में लाइन 10 के बाद लाइन 11 चलती है, सब प्रेडिक्टेबल होता है। लेकिन LLM में एक सवाल के पीछे 10 स्टेप्स हो सकते हैं — RAG सर्च, री-रैंकिंग, 3 प्रॉम्प्ट्स, टूल कॉल!
अगर बीच में कुछ गलत हुआ तो कैसे पता चलेगा?
यही Tracing करती है! वो हर स्टेप का एक्सरे निकालती है — 'सर्च ने क्या डॉक्यूमेंट निकाले? प्रॉम्प्ट क्या बना? मॉडल ने क्या सोचा? टूल ने क्या रिटर्न किया?'
यानी पूरी सोचने की प्रक्रिया एक पेड़ की तरह दिख जाती है!
बिल्कुल! LangSmith या OpenTelemetry से हम तुरंत पकड़ लेते हैं कि किस स्टेप पर गड़बड़ हुई।
scenes.question: What is LLM observability/tracing, and why is it different from traditional software observability?
scenes.interview_question: What is LLM observability/tracing, and why is it different from traditional software observability?
scenes.interview_view:
Traditional observability tracks deterministic code paths. LLM systems are non-deterministic and often multi-step (retrieval → re-ranking → generation → tool calls), requiring traces to capture the full reasoning path: every prompt, intermediate output, tool call and result, token counts, and latency at each hop. This granularity, provided by tools like LangSmith, Langfuse, and Arize Phoenix, is crucial for debugging, unlike off-the-shelf APM tools.

scenes.title: Safely Rolling Out LLM Changes
scenes.teaching_intent: To teach best practices for safely deploying changes to prompts or model versions in production, emphasizing rigorous testing and gradual rollouts.
scenes.necessity: LLM behavior is complex and sensitive. Changes to prompts or models can easily introduce regressions or unexpected behaviors, making careful deployment crucial to avoid breaking production.
scenes.story: You've found a clever way to tweak a prompt that fixes a really annoying edge case in your LLM application. You're excited, you push it to production, and then... crickets. Or worse, customer support calls start flooding in because your 'fix' accidentally broke ten other common scenarios that were working fine before. This is a very real problem with LLMs, where small changes can have big, unpredictable consequences.
scenes.narration:
जब हम प्रॉम्प्ट या मॉडल का नया वर्जन लाएं, तो उसे सेफली कैसे रिलीज करें?
कभी भी एक झटके में 100% यूजर्स के लिए मत बदलो दोस्त! AI बहुत अनप्रिडिक्टेबल होता है, हो सकता है नया प्रॉम्प्ट किसी पुराने केस को बिगाड़ दे।
तो क्या तरीका अपनाएं?
पहले एक Evaluation Suite पर टेस्ट करो — कम से कम 200 सवालों का सेट। अगर वो पास हो, तो Canary Release करो — सिर्फ 5% यूजर्स को नया मॉडल दिखाओ।
और अगर सब ठीक रहे तभी आगे बढ़ें?

scenes.interview_question: How do you safely roll out a change to a prompt or model version in a production LLM application?

Then, roll out gradually via canary or A/B testing on a small percentage of live traffic, monitoring key signals, and ensuring an instant rollback path. Prompts should be under version control with a regression suite that runs automatically on every change.

scenes.title: Designing Fallback and Failover for LLM Providers
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain the necessity and implementation of robust fallback and failover mechanisms when relying on external LLM providers, ensuring application resilience.
scenes.necessity: External LLM providers can experience outages or rate limiting, which can completely cripple an application. Designing fallbacks is crucial for maintaining availability and a graceful user experience.
scenes.story: Imagine your entire LLM application relies on a single external provider. What happens if their API goes down for an hour? Or if your usage suddenly spikes, and you hit their rate limits? Your entire application grinds to a halt, users get errors, and your business takes a hit. Relying on a single point of failure is incredibly risky. This is where the idea of 'fallback' becomes absolutely necessary.
scenes.narration:
अगर OpenAI या Anthropic का सर्वर डाउन हो जाए, तो हमारी ऐप बंद न हो, इसके लिए क्या करें?
दोस्त, कभी भी सिर्फ एक प्रोवाइडर के भरोसे मत बैठो! इसे कहते हैं Fallback and Failover आर्किटेक्चर।
मतलब अगर एक बंद हो, तो दूसरा तुरंत संभाल ले?
हाँ! तुम्हारी ऐप में प्राइमरी प्रोवाइडर OpenAI हो सकता है, लेकिन अगर उसने 500 एरर दिया या रेट-लिमिट किया, तो कोड अपने आप Anthropic या AWS Bedrock पर स्विच हो जाए।
लेकिन दोनों के प्रॉम्प्ट अलग हो सकते हैं?

scenes.title: Implementing Streaming Responses for Better UX
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain how streaming responses work in LLM applications and why they are crucial for improving perceived latency and user experience.
scenes.necessity: LLM generation can take several seconds, leading to a poor user experience if the user has to wait for the entire response. Streaming improves perceived responsiveness.
scenes.story: Imagine you ask an AI a complex question. If you have to wait 10 whole seconds for the complete answer to appear all at once, it feels slow, right? Now, imagine another AI that starts typing out its response immediately, token by token, even if it still takes 10 seconds total to finish. Which one feels faster and more responsive? The second one, hands down. That's the magic of streaming.
scenes.narration:
Streaming Responses क्यों जरूरी हैं? क्या इससे स्पीड बढ़ जाती है?
असल स्पीड नहीं बढ़ती दोस्त, लेकिन यूजर को बहुत सुकून मिलता है! सोचो तुमने एक लंबा सवाल पूछा और स्क्रीन पर 10 सेकंड तक सिर्फ एक पहिया घूम रहा है।
यूजर सोचेगा कि ऐप हैंग हो गई!
एक्जेक्टली! लेकिन अगर पहले ही सेकंड में एक-एक शब्द टाइप होता हुआ दिखने लगे (SSE यानी Server-Sent Events के जरिए), तो यूजर तुरंत पढ़ना शुरू कर देता है।

scenes.title: LLM-as-judge: Scaling Evaluation
scenes.teaching_intent: To make the learner understand the practical need for automated LLM evaluation and its inherent challenges.
scenes.necessity: Evaluating the quality of LLM outputs at scale is a huge bottleneck. Manual human review is slow, expensive, and doesn't scale for the vast number of outputs a production LLM generates.
scenes.story: Imagine you're running a massive online service that uses an LLM to generate personalized responses for millions of users every day. How do you check if all those responses are actually good, helpful, or correct? You can't hire enough people to read every single one, right? The sheer volume makes it impossible. Yahin par the real problem starts.
scenes.narration:
LLM-as-a-judge क्या है? क्या एक AI दूसरे AI के काम को चेक कर सकता है?
बिल्कुल! जब तुम्हारे पास 10,000 टेस्ट सवाल हों, तो इंसान बैठकर हर जवाब को चेक नहीं कर सकता — बहुत महंगा पड़ेगा।
तो हम GPT-4 को जज बना देते हैं?
हाँ! हम उसे दोनों जवाब दिखाते हैं और एक सख्त रूब्रिक (नियमों की लिस्ट) देते हैं। वो 1 से 5 स्टार रेटिंग देता है और वजह भी बताता है।
लेकिन क्या जज में कोई पक्षपात यानी Bias भी होता है?
हाँ! पोजीशन बायस (जो जवाब पहले लिखा हो उसे ज्यादा नंबर देना) और वर्बोसिटी बायस (लंबे जवाब को बिना वजह अच्छा समझना)। इसलिए दोनों जवाबों की जगह बदलकर दो बार टेस्ट करते हैं!
scenes.question: So, how do we efficiently evaluate LLM outputs at scale? And what are the hidden pitfalls in doing so? That's exactly what this question addresses: What is LLM-as-judge, and what are its known failure modes?
scenes.interview_question: So, how do we efficiently evaluate LLM outputs at scale? And what are the hidden pitfalls in doing so? That's exactly what this question addresses: What is LLM-as-judge, and what are its known failure modes?
scenes.interview_view:
LLM-as-judge uses a (typically stronger) LLM to evaluate the outputs of another LLM against a rubric — e.g., scoring helpfulness, correctness, or faithfulness — which scales far better than manual human review and is now standard for offline eval pipelines and even some online quality monitoring. Known failure modes include: position bias (favoring the first response when comparing two outputs), self-preference bias (judge model favors its own model family), verbosity bias (longer answers score higher regardless of quality), and sensitivity to rubric/prompt wording. Best practices involve validating the judge against human-labeled data, using clear rubrics, and combining scores with human spot-checks.

Interview perspective:
Interviewers usually care about the application boundary, not only the model. Separate untrusted input from system instructions, validate tool arguments server-side, enforce least privilege, protect sensitive data, log safely, and define explicit refusal/fallback paths.

How would you test this control against adversarial inputs?
What data should never appear in logs or traces?

scenes.title: Implementing Guardrails for GenAI Systems
scenes.teaching_intent: To explain why LLMs need external safety mechanisms beyond prompting, and categorize these 'guardrails'.
scenes.necessity: LLMs are powerful but can be unpredictable. Relying solely on prompting them to 'be good' is insufficient for production systems that need to enforce strict safety, correctness, and policy constraints.
scenes.story: Imagine you're building a state-of-the-art self-driving car. The car's AI is incredibly smart, but would you ever let it drive on its own without any safety features like airbags, seatbelts, or even physical barriers on the road? Of course not! You need external safeguards.
scenes.narration:
Guardrails क्या होते हैं? ये हमारे AI ऐप के दरबान कैसे हैं?
दोस्त, जैसे किसी मॉल के गेट पर सिक्योरिटी गार्ड होता है जो चेक करता है कि कोई हथियार तो नहीं ला रहा — Guardrails वही काम करते हैं!
ये क्या-क्या चेक करते हैं?
इनपुट गार्डरेल चेक करता है कि यूजर कोई जेलब्रेक, गालियां, या हैकिंग प्रॉम्प्ट तो नहीं भेज रहा। और आउटपुट गार्डरेल चेक करता है कि मॉडल ने गलती से कोई गाली, गलत सलाह, या PII तो लीक नहीं कर दी!
कौन से टूल्स यूज़ होते हैं इसके लिए?
NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard, और Guardrails AI! ये प्रोडक्शन में सुरक्षा की पक्की दीवार हैं।
scenes.question: Similarly, with LLMs, how do we ensure they don't go 'off-road' and generate harmful content, leak sensitive data, or get tricked by malicious users? That's the problem guardrails solve. So, what are guardrails, and what are the main categories you'd implement in a production GenAI system?
scenes.interview_question: Similarly, with LLMs, how do we ensure they don't go 'off-road' and generate harmful content, leak sensitive data, or get tricked by malicious users? That's the problem guardrails solve. So, what are guardrails, and what are the main categories you'd implement in a production GenAI system?
scenes.interview_view:
Guardrails are checks placed around an LLM's inputs and/or outputs to enforce safety, correctness, and policy constraints beyond what prompting alone reliably guarantees. Input guardrails include PII detection/redaction, prompt injection/jailbreak detection, topic/scope filtering, and rate limiting/abuse detection. Output guardrails include toxicity/harmful content filtering, structured output validation, factuality/groundedness checks for RAG answers, and PII leakage checks. Architecturally, these are usually implemented as separate lightweight classifiers or rule-based checks that run before/after the main LLM call, not solely within the model's prompt.

Interview perspective:
Interviewers usually care about the application boundary, not only the model. Separate untrusted input from system instructions, validate tool arguments server-side, enforce least privilege, protect sensitive data, log safely, and define explicit refusal/fallback paths.

What data should never appear in logs or traces?

scenes.title: Securely Handling PII in GenAI Applications
scenes.teaching_intent: To highlight the critical importance of PII protection in GenAI and outline practical strategies for managing it.
scenes.necessity: GenAI applications often process user data that contains Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Mishandling PII can lead to severe privacy breaches, legal penalties, and loss of user trust.
scenes.story: Imagine you're building a customer support bot that helps users with their queries. These queries often contain names, email addresses, phone numbers – all PII. You can't just feed this raw data to a third-party LLM service, right? What if that service logs everything, or worse, uses it for its own training? That's a huge compliance and privacy nightmare.
scenes.narration:
PII यानी पर्सनली आइडेंटिफिएबल इंफॉर्मेशन को AI में कैसे संभालें?
दोस्त, कभी भी यूजर का आधार कार्ड नंबर, फोन नंबर, या क्रेडिट कार्ड नंबर सीधे LLM को मत भेजो! ये बहुत बड़ा प्राइवेसी कानून का उल्लंघन है।
तो फिर क्या करें?
Microsoft Presidio जैसे टूल से PII को Redact यानी छुपा दो! जैसे 'रोहन का फोन नंबर 9876543210 है' को बदलकर कर दो '[NAME] का फोन नंबर [PHONE_NUMBER] है'।
और जवाब आने के बाद?
जवाब आने के बाद वापस असली नाम लगाकर यूजर को दिखा दो। इससे मॉडल को असली डेटा का पता भी नहीं चला और काम भी हो गया!
scenes.question: So, how do we responsibly and securely manage PII when designing GenAI applications that interact with user data? This leads to the question: How do you handle PII in a GenAI application that processes user data?
